PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

gufuncs","user":{"login":"izaid","id":482179,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjQ4MjE3OQ==","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/482179?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid","html_url":"https://github.com/izaid","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"This PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

+import math
+
+import numpy as np
+
+import pytest
+from numpy.testing import (assert_equal, assert_almost_equal, assert_array_almost_equal,
+    assert_, assert_allclose)
+
+from scipy import special
+
+# Base polynomials come from Abrahmowitz and Stegan
+class TestLegendre:
+    def test_legendre(self):
+        leg0 = special.legendre(0)
+        leg1 = special.legendre(1)
+        leg2 = special.legendre(2)
+        leg3 = special.legendre(3)
+        leg4 = special.legendre(4)
+        leg5 = special.legendre(5)
+        assert_equal(leg0.c, [1])
+        assert_equal(leg1.c, [1,0])
+        assert_almost_equal(leg2.c, np.array([3,0,-1])/2.0, decimal=13)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg3.c, np.array([5,0,-3,0])/2.0)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg4.c, np.array([35,0,-30,0,3])/8.0)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg5.c, np.array([63,0,-70,0,15,0])/8.0)
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('n', [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('zr', [0.5241717, 12.80232, -9.699001,
+                                    0.5122437, 0.1714377])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('zi', [9.766818, 0.2999083, 8.24726, -22.84843,
+                                    -0.8792666])
+    def test_lpn_against_clpmn(self, n, zr, zi):
+        reslpn = special.lpn(n, zr + zi*1j)
+        resclpmn = special.clpmn(0, n, zr+zi*1j)
+        assert_allclose(reslpn[0], resclpmn[0][0])
+        assert_allclose(reslpn[1], resclpmn[1][0])
+
+class TestLegendreP:
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", [(10,), (4, 9), (3, 5, 7)])
+    def test_ode(self, shape):
+        rng = np.random.default_rng(1234)
+
+        n = rng.integers(0, 100, shape)
+        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, shape)
+
+        p, p_jac, p_hess = special.legendre_p(n, x, diff_n = 2)
+
+        assert p.shape == shape
+        assert p_jac.shape == p.shape
+        assert p_hess.shape == p_jac.shape
+
+        err = (1 - x * x) * p_hess - 2 * x * p_jac + n * (n + 1) * p
+        np.testing.assert_allclose(err, 0, atol = 1e-10)
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("n_max", [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("x_shape", [(10,), (4, 9), (3, 5, 7)])
+    def test_all_ode(self, n_max, x_shape):
+        rng = np.random.default_rng(1234)
+
+        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, x_shape)
+        p, p_jac, p_hess = special.legendre_p_all(n_max, x, diff_n = 2)
+
+        n = np.arange(n_max + 1)
+        n = np.expand_dims(n, axis = tuple(range(1, x.ndim + 1)))
+
+        assert p.shape == (len(n),) + x.shape
+        assert p_jac.shape == p.shape
+        assert p_hess.shape == p_jac.shape
+
+        err = (1 - x * x) * p_hess - 2 * x * p_jac + n * (n + 1) * p
+        np.testing.assert_allclose(err, 0, atol = 1e-10)
+
+    def test_legacy(self):
+        p, pd = special.lpn(2, 0.5)
+        assert_array_almost_equal(p, [1.00000, 0.50000, -0.12500], 4)
+        assert_array_almost_equal(pd, [0.00000, 1.00000, 1.50000], 4)

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

+import collections
+import numbers
+import numpy as np
+
+from ._input_validation import _nonneg_int_or_fail
+
+from ._special_ufuncs import (legendre_p, assoc_legendre_p,
+                              sph_legendre_p, sph_harm_y)
+from ._gufuncs import (legendre_p_all, assoc_legendre_p_all,
+                       sph_legendre_p_all, sph_harm_y_all)
+
+__all__ = [
+    "assoc_legendre_p",
+    "assoc_legendre_p_all",
+    "legendre_p",
+    "legendre_p_all",
+    "sph_harm_y",
+    "sph_harm_y_all",
+    "sph_legendre_p",
+    "sph_legendre_p_all",
+]
+
+
+class MultiUFunc:
+    def __init__(self, ufunc_or_ufuncs, doc=None, *,
+                 force_complex_output=False, **default_kwargs):
+        if not isinstance(ufunc_or_ufuncs, np.ufunc):
+            if isinstance(ufunc_or_ufuncs, collections.abc.Mapping):
+                ufuncs_iter = ufunc_or_ufuncs.values()
+            elif isinstance(ufunc_or_ufuncs, collections.abc.Iterable):
+                ufuncs_iter = ufunc_or_ufuncs
+            else:
+                raise ValueError("ufunc_or_ufuncs should be a ufunc or a"
+                                 " ufunc collection")
+
+            # Perform input validation to ensure all ufuncs in ufuncs are
+            # actually ufuncs and all take the same input types.
+            seen_input_types = set()
+            for ufunc in ufuncs_iter:
+                if not isinstance(ufunc, np.ufunc):
+                    raise ValueError("All ufuncs must have"
+                                     f" type `numpy.ufunc`. Received {ufunc_or_ufuncs}")
+                seen_input_types.add(frozenset(x.split("->")[0] for x in ufunc.types))
+            if len(seen_input_types) > 1:
+                raise ValueError("All ufuncs must take the same input types.")
+
+        self._ufunc_or_ufuncs = ufunc_or_ufuncs
+        self.__doc = doc
+        self.__force_complex_output = force_complex_output
+        self._default_kwargs = default_kwargs
+        self.resolve_out_shapes = None
+        self.key = None
+        self.ufunc_default_args = lambda *args, **kwargs: ()
+        self.ufunc_default_kwargs = lambda *args, **kwargs: {}
+
+    @property
+    def __doc__(self):
+        return self.__doc
+
+    @property
+    def force_complex_output(self):
+        return self.__force_complex_output
+
+    def override_key(self, func):
+        """Set `key` method by decorating a function.
+        """
+        self.key = func
+
+    def override_ufunc_default_args(self, func):
+        self.ufunc_default_args = func
+
+    def override_ufunc_default_kwargs(self, func):
+        self.ufunc_default_kwargs = func
+
+    def override_resolve_out_shapes(self, func):
+        """Set `resolve_out_shapes` method by decorating a function."""
+        if func.__doc__ is None:
+            func.__doc__ = \
+                """Resolve to output shapes based on relevant inputs."""
+        func.__name__ = "resolve_out_shapes"
+        self.resolve_out_shapes = func
+
+    def resolve_ufunc(self, **kwargs):
+        """Resolve to a ufunc based on keyword arguments."""
+
+        if isinstance(self._ufunc_or_ufuncs, np.ufunc):
+            return self._ufunc_or_ufuncs
+
+        ufunc_key = self.key(**kwargs)
+        return self._ufunc_or_ufuncs[ufunc_key]
+
+    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
+        kwargs = self._default_kwargs | kwargs
+
+        args += self.ufunc_default_args(**kwargs)
+
+        ufunc = self.resolve_ufunc(**kwargs)
+
+        ufunc_args = args[-ufunc.nin:] # array arguments to be passed to the ufunc
+
+        ufunc_kwargs = self.ufunc_default_kwargs(**kwargs)
+
+        if (self.resolve_out_shapes is not None):
+            ufunc_arg_shapes = tuple(np.shape(ufunc_arg) for ufunc_arg in ufunc_args)
+            ufunc_out_shapes = self.resolve_out_shapes(*args[:-ufunc.nin],
+                *ufunc_arg_shapes, ufunc.nout)
+
+            ufunc_arg_dtypes = tuple((ufunc_arg.dtype if hasattr(ufunc_arg, 'dtype')
+                else np.dtype(type(ufunc_arg))) for ufunc_arg in ufunc_args)
+            if hasattr(ufunc, 'resolve_dtypes'):
+                ufunc_dtypes = ufunc_arg_dtypes + ufunc.nout * (None,)
+                ufunc_dtypes = ufunc.resolve_dtypes(ufunc_dtypes) 
+                ufunc_out_dtypes = ufunc_dtypes[-ufunc.nout:]
+            else:
+                ufunc_out_dtype = np.result_type(*ufunc_arg_dtypes)
+                if (not np.issubdtype(ufunc_out_dtype, np.inexact)):
+                    ufunc_out_dtype = np.float64
+
+                ufunc_out_dtypes = ufunc.nout * (ufunc_out_dtype,)
+
+            if self.force_complex_output:
+                ufunc_out_dtypes = tuple(np.result_type(1j, ufunc_out_dtype)
+                    for ufunc_out_dtype in ufunc_out_dtypes)
+
+            out = tuple(np.empty(ufunc_out_shape, dtype = ufunc_out_dtype)
+                for ufunc_out_shape, ufunc_out_dtype
+                in zip(ufunc_out_shapes, ufunc_out_dtypes))
+
+            ufunc_kwargs['out'] = out
+
+        return ufunc(*ufunc_args, **ufunc_kwargs)
+

+sph_legendre_p = MultiUFunc(sph_legendre_p,
+    r"""sph_legendre_p(n, m, phi, *, diff_n=0)
+
+    Spherical Legendre polynomial of the first kind.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    n : array_like, int
+        Order of the Legendre polynomial, must have ``n >= 0``.
+    m : array_like, int
+        Degree of the Legendre polynomial.
+    phi : array_like, float
+        Input value.
+    diff_n : Optional[int]
+        A non-negative integer. Compute and return all derivatives up
+        to order ``diff_n``.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    p : ndarray or tuple[ndarray]
+        The spherical Legendre polynomial with ``diff_n`` derivatives.
+
+    Notes
+    -----
+    With respect to the associated Legendre polynomial :math:`P_{m}^{n}(\cos \phi)`,
+    the spherical Legendre polynomial is defined as
+
+    .. math::
+
+        \sqrt{\frac{(2 n + 1) (n - m)!}{4 \pi (n + m)!}} P_{n}^{m}(\cos \phi)
+
+    This is the same as the spherical harmonic :math:`Y_{m}^{n}(\theta, \phi)`
+    with :math:`\theta = 0`.
+    """, diff_n=0
+)
+
+
+@sph_legendre_p.override_key
+def _(diff_n):
+    diff_n = _nonneg_int_or_fail(diff_n, "diff_n", strict=False)
+    if not 0 <= diff_n <= 2:
+        raise ValueError(
+            "diff_n is currently only implemented for orders 0, 1, and 2,"
+            f" received: {diff_n}."
+        )
+    return diff_n
+

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

PR demonstrates a way forward for special functions defined by recurrence relations, as well as some other issues with special functions more generally. Here we will use the Legendre polynomials `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` as illustrative examples, and the work has been done for these functions.

As has been discussed extensively elsewhere, a good model for special functions is C / C++ kernels published to Python as NumPy universal functions [1]. Even the more complicated functions that need to operate on subarrays, like the Legendre polynomials being discussed here, fit into this model as generalized universal functions [2]. By refactoring the existing special functions to be ufuncs, we are also able to provide the scalar kernels to other array libraries, so our model is more general than just NumPy on the CPU.

An unsolved question so far is then how to handle _variants_ of the normal behaviour. This is necessary for some of the more complicated special functions and hasn't been properly solved before. Consider the associated Legendre polynomial `lpmn` for instance. It should be able to support:

- Returning either the normalized or unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials. Currently only the unnormalized associated Legendre polynomials are available in SciPy, but everyone else (Julia, MATLAB, ...) supports normalization. Why does SciPy not?
- Returning derivatives, also up to different orders. Currently `lpmn` has to return both the polynomials `Pmn_z` and their derivatives `Pmn_d_z`. There is no option to not return the derivative. And throughout the special functions there are many different adhoc conventions for keywords that return derivatives.
- Returning all the values computed throughout the recurrence. These pairs of "at" versus "all" functions have already been discussed a lot [4].

Here I have refactored `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` in both C++ and Python so that all these things can be supported easily. The C++ code is important but, for the purposes of SciPy, it is a private implementation. In Python, there are a couple of changes to the public SciPy API in the `special` module. I will describe everything below.

_Python API changes._
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` all gain a keyword `diff_n` that indicates the order of derivatives to return. It defaults to 0, but can be 1 or 2. All derivatives up to that order are returned, so `diff_n = 2` gives you 3 outputs. This is just what makes sense for Legendre polynomials. Note I am happy to change the name of this keyword if suggested.
- The "all" versions of `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` are introduced as `lpn_all`, `lpmn_all`, and `clpmn_all`. I thought long and hard about whether they should be in like that or as a keyword similar to `mode = "at"` or `mode = "all"`. Given how things are implemented, it just doesn't make a lot of sense to use a keyword here, so I've gone with separate functions.
- `lpn`, `lpmn`, and `clpmn` historically have returned the "all" versions, but will become the "at" versions going forward. There is a keyword `legacy` that defaults to `True` to switch the behaviour. There will need to be a deprecation cycle.
- `lpmn` and `clpmn` also gain a keyword `norm` which can be either `True` or `False` to return the normalised or unnormalised Legendre polynomials. I still have to implement the normalisation, but that will come once everyone is happy with all of this.

_C++ implementation_
- To support all these different variants (derivative or not, "all" or "at", and so on), I have rewritten the C++ algorithms to take a C++ callback. This callback is called at each recurrence step and can be fully custom. I've added callback functions to work out the derivatives and callbacks to store all the recurrence values in a subarray, this is how we can support all these different behaviours without writing the same algorithm many times. It should be effectively zero cost as C++ allows templating on the callback type, which is what I have done. The `lpn` C++ code is a clear example of how this works, see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/special/legendre.h#L22.
- Not all behaviour can be added on like that, and normalisation is a good case where it is just a different function.
- `clpmn` and `lpmn` have been merged into one function, but defaulting to different branch cuts just like SciPy currently does.
- Each pair of `diff_n` and `norm` is published to Python as a ufunc. In this case, they are collected using `Py_BuildValue` as a dictionary of tuples. So essentially what we have is a simple and minimal collection of ufuncs that encapsulates all the behaviour variants.

_Python implementation_
- At the Python level, I have introduced a minimal class called `multiufunc`. This is only intended to be used for these special functions with complicated behaviour, and will behave like a ufunc as much as possible. It has a very simple model.
- In a `multiufunc`, keywords can be used to select the right ufunc from the collection of ufuncs. So `lpmn(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` will use `norm` and `diff_n` to select a ufunc that computes the normalised Legendre polynomials and their derivative. Additional positional arguments that precede the array arguments can be used to allocate the output, as `lpmn_all(m, n, x, norm = True, diff_n = 1)` needs to allocate output arrays of shape `(2 m + 1, n, ...)`.
- There are no "special" keywords, it is just convention. So `diff_n` has no special meaning and is not builtin to the `multiufunc` class or anything like that.
- You can see how this works for `lpmn` at https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/79421615dc66425bc47899f2afe254f5c7284398/scipy/special/_basic.py#L1727

I know this is a lot of information. I've been thinking and working on how to solve these problems for a long time. My guiding principle has been to _keep the fundamental model of computation a ufunc_ and build on top of that. Happy to discuss and elaborate more.

+import math
+
+import numpy as np
+
+import pytest
+from numpy.testing import (assert_equal, assert_almost_equal, assert_array_almost_equal,
+    assert_, assert_allclose)
+
+from scipy import special
+
+# Base polynomials come from Abrahmowitz and Stegan
+class TestLegendre:
+    def test_legendre(self):
+        leg0 = special.legendre(0)
+        leg1 = special.legendre(1)
+        leg2 = special.legendre(2)
+        leg3 = special.legendre(3)
+        leg4 = special.legendre(4)
+        leg5 = special.legendre(5)
+        assert_equal(leg0.c, [1])
+        assert_equal(leg1.c, [1,0])
+        assert_almost_equal(leg2.c, np.array([3,0,-1])/2.0, decimal=13)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg3.c, np.array([5,0,-3,0])/2.0)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg4.c, np.array([35,0,-30,0,3])/8.0)
+        assert_almost_equal(leg5.c, np.array([63,0,-70,0,15,0])/8.0)
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('n', [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('zr', [0.5241717, 12.80232, -9.699001,
+                                    0.5122437, 0.1714377])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize('zi', [9.766818, 0.2999083, 8.24726, -22.84843,
+                                    -0.8792666])
+    def test_lpn_against_clpmn(self, n, zr, zi):
+        reslpn = special.lpn(n, zr + zi*1j)
+        resclpmn = special.clpmn(0, n, zr+zi*1j)
+        assert_allclose(reslpn[0], resclpmn[0][0])
+        assert_allclose(reslpn[1], resclpmn[1][0])
+
+class TestLegendreP:
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", [(10,), (4, 9), (3, 5, 7)])
+    def test_ode(self, shape):
+        rng = np.random.default_rng(1234)
+
+        n = rng.integers(0, 100, shape)
+        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, shape)
+
+        p, p_jac, p_hess = special.legendre_p(n, x, diff_n = 2)
+
+        assert p.shape == shape
+        assert p_jac.shape == p.shape
+        assert p_hess.shape == p_jac.shape
+
+        err = (1 - x * x) * p_hess - 2 * x * p_jac + n * (n + 1) * p
+        np.testing.assert_allclose(err, 0, atol = 1e-10)
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("n_max", [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32])
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("x_shape", [(10,), (4, 9), (3, 5, 7)])
+    def test_all_ode(self, n_max, x_shape):
+        rng = np.random.default_rng(1234)
+
+        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, x_shape)
+        p, p_jac, p_hess = special.legendre_p_all(n_max, x, diff_n = 2)
+
+        n = np.arange(n_max + 1)
+        n = np.expand_dims(n, axis = tuple(range(1, x.ndim + 1)))
+
+        assert p.shape == (len(n),) + x.shape
+        assert p_jac.shape == p.shape
+        assert p_hess.shape == p_jac.shape
+
+        err = (1 - x * x) * p_hess - 2 * x * p_jac + n * (n + 1) * p
+        np.testing.assert_allclose(err, 0, atol = 1e-10)
+
+    def test_legacy(self):
+        p, pd = special.lpn(2, 0.5)
+        assert_array_almost_equal(p, [1.00000, 0.50000, -0.12500], 4)
+        assert_array_almost_equal(pd, [0.00000, 1.00000, 1.50000], 4)

+def assoc_legendre_factor(n, m, norm):
+    if norm:
+        return math.sqrt((2 * n + 1) * \
+            math.factorial(n - m) / (2 * math.factorial(n + m)))
+
+    return 1
+
+def assoc_legendre_p_0_0(z, *, typ, norm = False):
+    fac = assoc_legendre_factor(0, 0, norm)
+
+    return np.full_like(z, fac)
+
+def assoc_legendre_p_1_0(z, *, typ, norm = False):
+    fac = assoc_legendre_factor(1, 0, norm)
+
+    return fac * z
+
+def assoc_legendre_p_1_1(z, *, typ, norm = False):
+    branch_sign = np.where(typ == 3, np.where(np.signbit(np.real(z)), 1, -1), -1)
+    typ_sign = np.where(typ == 3, -1, 1)
+    fac = assoc_legendre_factor(1, 1, norm)
+
+    w = np.sqrt(np.where(typ == 3, z * z - 1, 1 - z * z))
+
+    return typ_sign * branch_sign * fac * w
+
+def assoc_legendre_p_1_m1(z, *, typ, norm = False):
+    typ_sign = np.where(typ == 3, -1, 1)
+    fac = assoc_legendre_factor(1, -1, norm)
+
+    return -typ_sign * fac * \
+        assoc_legendre_p_1_1(z, typ = typ) / 2
