I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. +/*

+ * arithmetic package based on David Bailey's Fortran-90 double-double
+ * package, with some changes. See
+ *
+ *   http://www.nersc.gov/~dhbailey/mpdist/mpdist.html
+ *
+ * for the original Fortran-90 version.
+ *
+ * Overall structure is similar to that of Keith Brigg's C++ double-double

+ *
+ *   http://www-epidem.plansci.cam.ac.uk/~kbriggs/doubledouble.html
+ *

+/*

+        /* volatile is used below to prevent aggressive optimizations which may change

+         */
+
+        /* Computes fl(a+b) and err(a+b).  Assumes |a| >= |b|. */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double quick_two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {
+            volatile double s = a + b;
+            volatile double c = s - a;
+            *err = b - c;
+            return s;
+        }
+
+        /* Computes fl(a+b) and err(a+b).  */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {
+            volatile double s = a + b;
+            volatile double c = s - a;
+            volatile double d = b - c;
+            volatile double e = s - c;
+            *err = (a - e) + d;
+            return s;
+        }
+
+        /* Computes fl(a*b) and err(a*b). */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_prod(double a, double b, double *err) {
+            volatile double p = a * b;
+            *err = std::fma(a, b, -p);
+            return p;
+        }
+
+        /* Computes fl(a*a) and err(a*a).  Faster than the above method. */

+            }
+            return std::floor(d + 0.5);
+        }

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. +        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double quick_two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {

+            volatile double c = s - a;
+            *err = b - c;
+            return s;
+        }
+
+        /* Computes fl(a+b) and err(a+b).  */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {

+            volatile double c = s - a;
+            volatile double d = b - c;

+        }

+        /* Computes fl(a*b) and err(a*b). */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_prod(double a, double b, double *err) {

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. + *     n     -inf < x < inf         n
+ *
+ *
+ *                  [n(1-d)]
+ *        +            -                    v-1              n-v
+ *    Pr{D   > d} =    >    C    d (d + v/n)    (1 - d - v/n)
+ *        n            -   n v

+ *
+ * (also equals the following sum, but note the terms may be large and alternating in sign)
+ * See Smirnov 1944, Dwass 1959
+ *                         n

+ *                =  1 -   >         C    d (d + v/n)    (1 - d - v/n)

+ *
+ * [n(1-d)] is the largest integer not exceeding n(1-d).

+ * Sources:

I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double quick_two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {

+            return s;
+        }

+        /* Computes fl(a+b) and err(a+b).  */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {

+        }

+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_prod(double a, double b, double *err) {

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. The old cephes has been removed entirely. I've rewritten this PR message since the original I wrote when this was a work-in-progress is no longer relevant.*

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

You have your work cut out for you @izaid. +        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double quick_two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {

+            volatile double c = s - a;

+        }

+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_sum(double a, double b, double *err) {
+            volatile double s = a + b;
+            volatile double c = s - a;
+            volatile double d = b - c;
+            volatile double e = s - c;
+            *err = (a - e) + d;
+            return s;
+        }
+
+        /* Computes fl(a*b) and err(a*b). */
+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_prod(double a, double b, double *err) {
+            volatile double p = a * b;
+            *err = std::fma(a, b, -p);
+            return p;
+        }

+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_sqr(double a, double *err) {

+            *err = std::fma(a, a, -p);
+            return p;
+        }

+        SPECFUN_HOST_DEVICE inline double two_nint(double d) {

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

This PR translates the entirety of Cephes into C++ capable of running on CUDA through conditional compilation. This PR is rebased on #20405 which is rebased on #20089 which is rebased on #19954, so though still gargantuan, the true diff is a little smaller than what is seen now.

Most of this was fairly straightforward, there was just a lot of it. One challenge was translating double-double arithmetic from `cephes/dd_real.c` and friends (actually from the `qd` extended precision package) into C++. I chose to do this in a more modern style with operator overloading.

The old cephes has been removed entirely. I wrote C wrappers for use in Cython and C files which have not been translated to C++. `special_c_wrappers.cpp` for special functions, and `dd_real_wrappers.cpp` for double double arithmetic, which is used in `_cunity.pxd` and which has test code written in Cython.

In the recent nightly release, `special.jv` unexpectedly promotes float32 inputs to float64

### Reproducing Code Example

```python

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import jv

x = np.array([3], dtype='float32')
print(scipy.__version__)
print(jv(4, x).dtype)
```

Output in 1.13 release:
```
1.13.0
float32
```
Output in the most recent nightly release:
```
1.14.0.dev0+751.579a5bf
float64
```

intention is to update `cython_special` to go along with our general modernisation of `special`

Back in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260, we updated the ufunc machinery so that there was no longer any need for autogenerated loop functions for ufuncs. This PR handles the complementary Cython generation. For `cython_special`, however, the process is *way* simpler. The functions in `cython_special` just provide Cython-level access to the scalar kernels. There is no need for any autogeneration really, hence we can just paste in the current autogenerated Cython file (`cython_special.pyx` and `cython_special.pxd`) and start modifying them.

This will allow us to start deleting ufuncs from `_generate_pyx.py`, meaning we will no longer be duplicating ufuncs. We will also not need to maintain all these C wrappers for each scalar kernel, which are being wrapped in Cython anyway. The goal is `cython_special` should be wrapping the functions directly, in a way that is easy to modify. Back in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260, we updated the ufunc machinery so that there was no longer any need for autogenerated loop functions for ufuncs. This PR handles the complementary Cython generation. For `cython_special`, however, the process is *way* simpler. The functions in `cython_special` just provide Cython-level access to the scalar kernels. There is no need for any autogeneration really, hence we can just paste in the current autogenerated Cython file (`cython_special.pyx` and `cython_special.pxd`) and start modifying them.

This will allow us to start deleting ufuncs from `_generate_pyx.py`, meaning we will no longer be duplicating ufuncs. We will also not need to maintain all these C wrappers for each scalar kernel, which are being wrapped in Cython anyway. The goal is `cython_special` should be wrapping the functions directly, in a way that is easy to modify. up on the licensing part of the proposed vendoring of `kokkos/mdspan`, which has an Apache 2.0 + LLVM runtime exception license (see gh-20334, https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20320#pullrequestreview-1969858082).

@steppi opened https://github.com/kokkos/mdspan/issues/321 upstream to inquire about relicensing, which _may_ be possible but isn't a fast decision apparently.

First some context (copied from the review comment linked above):

The Apache 2.0 license in `mdspan.h` seems incompatible with SciPy's BSD-3 license. See:
- http://scipy.github.io/devdocs/dev/core-dev/index.html#licensing
- http://scipy.github.io/devdocs/dev/hacking.html#license-considerations
- https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/8370#issuecomment-363592943

It's not completely impossible to reconsider the current ban on Apache 2.0, as indicated by the comment in the last link above, but it's a major decision with long-term consequences that, even if we drop GPLv2 compatibility, will complicate the project's licensing situation.

* * *

After reviewing the LLVM runtime exception clause, it seems clear that that does address the GPLv2 compatibility issue, so there is no problem there.

The other problem is source-level licensing. Right now we have a BSD-3 license for SciPy as a whole (see [LICENSE.text](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/main/LICENSE.txt)), and a large-ish set of licenses for vendored code (see [LICENSES_bundled.txt](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/main/LICENSES_bundled.txt)). All of the licenses for bundled code are BSD-3 compatible: various other BSD flavors, MIT, Boost, and Qhull (BSD-like) licenses.

The LLVM runtime exception part of the `kokkos/mdspan` license is only related to linking. So for the license expression one would need to use to describe all of SciPy, that's not very relevant. Introducing Apache 2.0 would complicate describing the license - but perhaps not by that much. Distros tend to already exhaustively search for licensing and copyright info and mash everything together ([example for Debian](https://metadata.ftp-master.debian.org/changelogs//main/s/scipy/scipy_1.10.1-2_copyright)). So while not ideal to add this new license, it _may_ be acceptable.

Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I am currently writing some code whose hot loop involves the repeated computation of Bessel's `jn` and `yn` functions for a few orders (`0..50`) and for a large number of points (~200k). Currently SciPy's functions (both in Python and Cython form) are unusably slow, the following one-liner takes tens of seconds on my desktop:

```python
timeit.timeit(lambda: jn([[x] for x in np.arange(51, dtype=int)], np.arange(1e-3, 200, 1e-3)))
```

while MATLAB's counterpart executes in around four seconds, giving an order of magnitude (and a half) between the two languages:

```MATLAB
clear all
x = 1e-3:1e-3:200;
J = zeros(50,length(x));
tic
for i = 0:50-1
    J(i+1,:) = besselj(i, x);
end
toc
```

From what I can gather both Matlab and SciPy use the AMOS package under the hood (with some cases falling back to Cephes) and so I'd expect the performance to be comparable.

How is the vectorization implemented? If it is expressed in terms of `np.vectorize` that'd partially explain the slowdown, from what I see AMOS's functions support computing more than one order/point at the same time and it'd be nice to exploit that interface to save some time.

I'm no NumPy/SciPy wizard so if you have a better idea of what's wrong (or what could be done) I'm all ears.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

special","user":{"login":"izaid","id":482179,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjQ4MjE3OQ==","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/482179?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid","html_url":"https://github.com/izaid","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/izaid/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"This PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

PR follows the [one](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260) merged yesterday about overhauling the ufunc machinery. The purpose here is to extend that slightly (and only slightly) so that SciPy special can support generalised ufuncs for some of its existing functions. In particular, I am thinking of all the functions in _specfun.pyx. These include the Legendre polynomials, Airy and Bessel function zeros, and so on. No doubt others will follow.

These functions differ from their counterparts in that their kernels may take arrays as their inputs or outputs. A canonical example is matrix multiplication over stacks of matrices. Here it is a bit simpler, essentially we have special functions that return outputs with one or more additional dimensions. Usually these additional dimensions corrrespond simply to a value `n` in the input, so we have a function producing an array of shape `(n, ...)`. Currently, these functions in SciPy only work for scalar input, so given a value `x` the output is an array of size n. But there is no reason to have such a restriction, we could easily be given an array `x` of shape `(d0, ..., dm)` and get output of shape `(n, d0, ..., dm)`. Here we introduce such functionality.

This is actually quite a small change. We need to use NumPy's generalised ufunc machinery, namely `PyUFunc_FromFuncAndDataAndSignature` and pass an appropriate signature. Let's focus on `lpn`. With the new machinery, this is just:
```
PyObject *_lpn = SpecFun_NewGUFunc({special::lpn}, 2, "_lpn", "docstring here", "()->(n),(n)");
PyModule_AddObjectRef(_special_ufuncs, "_lpn", _lpn);
```

Then, at the Cython / Python level, The Legendre polynomials `lpn` went from:
```
def lpn(int n, double z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """
    cdef double *ppn
    cdef double *ppd
    cdef cnp.npy_intp dims[1]
    dims[0] = n + 1

    pn = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    pd = cnp.PyArray_ZEROS(1, dims, cnp.NPY_FLOAT64, 0)
    ppn = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pn)
    ppd = <cnp.float64_t *>cnp.PyArray_DATA(pd)
    specfun_lpn(n, z, ppn, ppd)
    return pn, pd
```
to:
```
def lpn(n, z):
    """
    Compute Legendre polynomials Pn(x) and their derivatives
    Pn'(x). This is a wrapper for the function 'specfun_lpn'.
    """

    pn = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    pd = np.zeros((n + 1,) + np.shape(z), dtype = np.float64)
    return _lpn(z, out = (pn, pd))
```
This also has the additional benefit of eliminating the need for Cython in these functions.

The last change is at the C++ level. This one is perhaps mostly for @steppi to check out. We need a very simple struct or class that can act as the C++-equivalent of a view (pointer, shape, and strides). Although there is nothing yet in C++17, that is actually already accepted into later versions of the standard, namely [std::span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span) in C++20 and [std::mdspan](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/mdspan) in C++23. Since we only support C++17, we can either create our own versions of these or create another data structure that is equivalent. It is just pointer, shape, and strides. CuPy does exactly the latter.

In this PR I made my own `std::span`. The Legendre polynomials then become, in C++.
```
inline void lpn(double x, std::span<double> pn, std::span<double> pd) {
    specfun::lpn(pn.size() - 1, x, pn.data(), pd.data());
}
```
And the generalised ufunc is published as above.

Putting this here now for thoughts.

intention is to update `cython_special` to go along with our general modernisation of `special`

Back in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20260, we updated the ufunc machinery so that there was no longer any need for autogenerated loop functions for ufuncs. This PR handles the complementary Cython generation. For `cython_special`, however, the process is *way* simpler. The functions in `cython_special` just provide Cython-level access to the scalar kernels. There is no need for any autogeneration really, hence we can just paste in the current autogenerated Cython file (`cython_special.pyx` and `cython_special.pxd`) and start modifying them.

This will allow us to start deleting ufuncs from `_generate_pyx.py`, meaning we will no longer be duplicating ufuncs. We will also not need to maintain all these C wrappers for each scalar kernel, which are being wrapped in Cython anyway. The goal is `cython_special` should be wrapping the functions directly, in a way that is easy to modify.
